name: External KVM device identity and adjacent host-artifact correlation

attribution.legal_posture: Source-attributed vendor observation and defensive abstraction; named-person attribution and adjudicated fact require separate sources.

caveats: IP-KVMs and remote-management tools serve legitimate support, lab, accessibility, and outsourcing uses; their presence is a contextual signal requiring case evidence for fraudulent employment or DPRK affiliation.
Product-specific raw queries, commands, device values, IPs, and other brittle selectors are intentionally omitted.
ReliaQuest presents aggregate observations rather than case-by-case evidence.
Some recommended controls are practitioner guidance rather than independently measured detection efficacy.
The source publishes qualitative detector guidance; measured efficacy requires testing against legitimate applicant, staffing, accessibility, support, lab, and outsourcing workflows.

statements: Join USB or hardware inventory, local DNS or mDNS, process or command telemetry, display-profile changes, asset custody, and approved-support-tool inventory during the early-tenure observation window.
Alert on unapproved external-console device classes or artifact combinations rather than on mutable filenames alone; verify against procurement and accessibility exceptions.
Do not treat COBO or an RMM blocklist as sufficient. Validate that the assigned worker retains the device and review hardware-mediated control alongside sign-in, location, and role-expected activity.
For BYOD exceptions, use a managed virtual workspace or equivalent enforceable device-posture boundary rather than assuming endpoint telemetry exists.
limitations: Behavioral anomalies require corroboration and human review; no single applicant, API, KVM, RMM, device, or network event establishes shared control, fraud, nationality, or DPRK attribution.

statements: A worker or facilitator can combine hardware-mediated console control with software RMM, or substitute external KVM hardware when RMM is blocked; defenders may still observe device-enumeration or adjacent host artifacts.
limitations: ReliaQuest presents aggregate observations rather than case-by-case evidence.
IP-KVMs and remote-management tools have legitimate support, lab, accessibility, and outsourcing uses; their presence does not prove fraudulent employment or DPRK affiliation.
Some recommended controls are practitioner guidance rather than independently measured detection efficacy.

sources.support: ReliaQuest reports that IP-KVM devices can provide console control outside the host operating system and therefore may not leave the software footprint expected from ordinary remote-management tools. ReliaQuest publishes examples of host-visible traces in USB inventory, local name resolution, commands, and display-profile metadata associated with two IP-KVM families. ReliaQuest also reports actors renaming RMM and IP-KVM tooling as detection improves, and states that IP-KVM use is not exclusive to DPRK-linked workers
